Monolithic vs Microservices.exp:
Monolithic Architecture builds an application as a single, unified unit where all components (UI, business logic, data access) are tightly coupled and deployed together. This is the traditional approach — simple to develop, test, and deploy initially, but becomes difficult to maintain as the codebase grows.

Microservices Architecture decomposes the application into small, independent services that communicate over a network. Each service owns its data, can be deployed independently, and is built around a specific business capability.

Key Differences:

  • Deployment: Monolith = one deployable unit; Microservices = independently deployable services
  • Scaling: Monolith = scale entire app; Microservices = scale only what's needed
  • Team Structure: Monolith = teams by layer (frontend, backend, DB); Microservices = teams by business capability
  • Data: Monolith = shared database; Microservices = database per service
  • Communication: Monolith = in-memory function calls; Microservices = network calls (REST, gRPC, messaging)

Most successful microservices start as monoliths and are decomposed as the organization and codebase grow — a pattern known as the Monolith-First approach advocated by Martin Fowler and Sam Newman.

Architecture Patterns.exp:
Layered Architecture (N-Tier) organizes code into horizontal layers: Presentation (UI), Business Logic (services), Persistence (data access), and Database. Each layer has a specific responsibility and communicates only with adjacent layers.

Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters) places the business logic at the center (core domain). External systems (databases, APIs, UIs) connect through ports (interfaces) and adapters (implementations). This isolates business rules from infrastructure concerns.

Clean Architecture (by Robert C. Martin) extends hexagonal with dependency inversion: inner layers (entities, use cases) know nothing about outer layers (frameworks, databases). Dependencies point inward — outer layers depend on inner layers.

Event-Driven Architecture uses events as the primary communication mechanism. Services publish events when something happens (order.created), and other services consume those events asynchronously. This enables loose coupling and eventual consistency.

CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) separates read and write operations into different models. Commands handle writes (create, update, delete), while queries handle reads. This optimizes each side independently.

SOLID Principles.exp:
SOLID is a set of five design principles for writing maintainable, scalable object-oriented code:

  • S — Single Responsibility: A class should have one, and only one, reason to change.
  • O — Open/Closed: Open for extension, closed for modification. Add new behavior through inheritance/composition, not by changing existing code.
  • L — Liskov Substitution: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without breaking the system.
  • I — Interface Segregation: Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they don't use. Prefer small, focused interfaces over large, general-purpose ones.
  • D — Dependency Inversion: Depend on abstractions (interfaces), not concretions. High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules.

These principles are especially important in system design because they reduce coupling between components, making systems easier to understand, test, and evolve.

Domain-Driven Design.exp:
Domain-Driven Design (DDD) is an approach to software development that centers the design around the business domain and its logic. Key concepts from Eric Evans' book:

  • Ubiquitous Language: A shared language between developers and domain experts, used in code, discussions, and documentation.
  • Bounded Context: Each domain concept has a specific meaning within a bounded context. The same word ('Order') might mean different things in Sales vs Shipping contexts.
  • Entities: Objects with a distinct identity that persists over time (e.g., a User with an ID).
  • Value Objects: Objects defined by their attributes, not identity (e.g., an Address, Money).
  • Aggregates: A cluster of domain objects treated as a single unit. The Aggregate Root is the entry point (e.g., Order is the root containing OrderItems).
  • Domain Events: Events that domain experts care about (e.g., OrderShipped, PaymentReceived).

DDD is the foundation for microservices decomposition — each bounded context typically maps to one microservice.

Coupling & Cohesion.exp:
Coupling measures how dependent one module is on another. Low coupling is good — changes in one module don't cascade to others. Types from worst to best:

  • Content Coupling: One module modifies internal data of another (worst)
  • Common Coupling: Multiple modules share global data
  • Control Coupling: One module controls the behavior of another via flags
  • Stamp Coupling: Passing unnecessary data structures between modules
  • Data Coupling: Modules communicate only via simple parameters (best)

Cohesion measures how closely related the responsibilities of a single module are. High cohesion is good — all parts of a module work together toward a single purpose. Types from worst to best:

  • Coincidental Cohesion: Random functions grouped together (worst)
  • Logical Cohesion: Functions that are logically similar (e.g., all utils)
  • Temporal Cohesion: Functions grouped because they run at the same time
  • Procedural Cohesion: Functions grouped by execution order
  • Communicational Cohesion: Functions operating on the same data
  • Sequential Cohesion: Output of one function is input to another
  • Functional Cohesion: All functions contribute to a single purpose (best)

Goal: High cohesion, low coupling — the foundation of maintainable system design.

Scalability (Horizontal vs Vertical).exp:
Vertical Scaling (Scale Up) means adding more power to a single server — more CPU, RAM, faster disks. It's simpler (no code changes needed) but has hard limits (maximum server specs) and gets exponentially expensive at the high end.

Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out) means adding more servers to handle increased load. It's virtually unlimited but requires architectural changes: load balancers, distributed databases, stateless services, and handling of distributed system challenges.

When to use each:

  • Vertical: Simple applications, legacy systems, databases with strong consistency needs, when you need simplicity
  • Horizontal: Modern cloud-native apps, systems expecting growth, fault-tolerant architectures, cost optimization at scale

Most cloud architectures use a combination: vertical scaling for databases (with read replicas for horizontal read scaling) and horizontal scaling for stateless application servers.

Availability & Reliability.exp:
Availability is the percentage of time a system is operational and accessible. Measured in 'nines':

  • 99% (Two nines) = 87.6 hours downtime/year
  • 99.9% (Three nines) = 8.76 hours downtime/year
  • 99.99% (Four nines) = 52.56 minutes downtime/year
  • 99.999% (Five nines) = 5.26 minutes downtime/year

Reliability is the probability that a system will perform its intended function without failure over time. MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) and MTTR (Mean Time To Repair) are key metrics.

Strategies to improve availability:

  • Redundancy: Multiple instances across availability zones/regions
  • Failover: Automatic switch to standby on failure (active-passive or active-active)
  • Health Checks: Regular endpoint monitoring to detect failures
  • Graceful Degradation: System continues with reduced functionality when components fail
  • Bulkheads: Isolate components so failure doesn't cascade

The SLA (Service Level Agreement) defines the promised availability level, often with financial penalties for violations.

CAP Theorem.exp:
The CAP Theorem (Brewer's Theorem) states that a distributed data store can only provide two of three guarantees simultaneously:

  • C — Consistency: Every read receives the most recent write or an error. All nodes see the same data at the same time.
  • A — Availability: Every request receives a (non-error) response, without guarantee that it contains the most recent write. The system stays operational even if some nodes fail.
  • P — Partition Tolerance: The system continues to operate despite network partitions (messages being dropped/delayed between nodes).

Since network partitions are inevitable in distributed systems, you must choose between CP (Consistency + Partition Tolerance, sacrificing availability during partitions) or AP (Availability + Partition Tolerance, sacrificing consistency). In practice, many systems offer tunable consistency (e.g., Cassandra's consistency levels) or eventual consistency (the system converges over time).

Examples:

  • CP Systems: Traditional RDBMS (sacrifice availability), Zookeeper, etcd, HBase
  • AP Systems: DNS, Cassandra, CouchDB, Amazon DynamoDB (default)
  • CA (not possible in distributed systems): Single-node databases

Consistency Models.exp:
Consistency models define how and when updates to data become visible to subsequent operations:

  • Strong Consistency: After a write completes, all subsequent reads (on any node) see the latest value. Achieved via synchronous replication or distributed consensus (Paxos, Raft). Used in financial systems, user authentication.
  • Eventual Consistency: Given enough time without new updates, all replicas will converge to the same value. Reads may see stale data temporarily. Used in DNS, CDNs, social media feeds.
  • Causal Consistency: Operations that are causally related are seen in the correct order. Concurrent operations (unrelated) can be seen in any order. Used in collaborative editing.
  • Read-Your-Writes Consistency: After a user writes data, their subsequent reads will see that write (but other users may not). Used in user profiles, session data.
  • Monotonic Reads: If a user reads a value, subsequent reads will never return older data. Prevents the 'time travel' problem where you see a newer version then an older one.

Choosing the right consistency model is a key system design decision — stronger consistency means more coordination overhead, higher latency, and lower availability during partitions.

Latency vs Throughput.exp:
Latency is the time it takes for a single request to complete (response time). Measured in milliseconds. Throughput is the number of requests a system can handle per unit time (requests/second or transactions/second).

These are related but distinct metrics. A system with low latency might have low throughput if it can't handle concurrent requests. A system with high throughput might have high latency under load because of queuing.

Key Concepts:

  • P50, P95, P99 Latency: The 50th, 95th, and 99th percentile response times. P99 means 99% of requests are faster than this value. The long tail of slow requests matters more than the average.
  • Head-of-Line Blocking: A slow request blocking subsequent requests in a queue.
  • Concurrency vs Parallelism: Concurrency is handling multiple tasks (interleaved), parallelism is executing multiple tasks simultaneously (multi-core).
  • Amdahl's Law: The speedup of a system is limited by the portion that cannot be parallelized.

Optimization strategies:

  • For latency: caching, CDN, faster algorithms, connection pools, async I/O
  • For throughput: horizontal scaling, connection pooling, batch processing, async processing

Service Decomposition.exp:
Decomposing a monolithic application into microservices requires careful thought. Key strategies:

1. Decompose by Business Capability
Identify distinct business functions: Orders, Inventory, Shipping, Payments, Users, etc. Each becomes a service owned by a single team.

2. Decompose by Subdomain (DDD)
Use Domain-Driven Design's bounded contexts. Each bounded context becomes a service. Understand the core, supporting, and generic subdomains.

3. Strangler Fig Pattern
Gradually replace monolith functionality with microservices. Wrap old code behind interfaces, then replace piece by piece. Add new features as services, route traffic gradually.

Common Pitfalls:

  • Distributed Monolith: Services that are tightly coupled and must be deployed together — worst of both worlds
  • Chatty Communication: Too many network calls between services (aim for coarse-grained APIs)
  • Shared Database: Services sharing a database create hidden coupling
  • Over-Splitting: Too many small services create operational complexity

Start with fewer, larger services and split as needed. A good starting size is a service that a single team can own and maintain.

API Gateway Pattern.exp:
An API Gateway is a single entry point for all client requests to a microservices system. It handles:

  • Routing: Directs requests to the appropriate service
  • Authentication: Verifies tokens centrally before requests reach services
  • Rate Limiting: Prevents abuse by throttling requests
  • Aggregation: Combines responses from multiple services into one response (reduces client roundtrips)
  • Protocol Translation: Converts between protocols (HTTP to gRPC, REST to GraphQL)
  • Load Balancing: Distributes requests across service instances
  • Caching: Caches responses to reduce load on services

Popular API Gateway solutions: Kong, NGINX Plus, AWS API Gateway, Azure API Management, Envoy (as sidecar), and custom gateways built with Express/Spring Cloud Gateway.

The Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern extends this: each client type (web, mobile, IoT) gets its own gateway optimized for its needs. A mobile BFF might return smaller payloads, while a web BFF might include more detail.

Service Mesh & Sidecar.exp:
A Service Mesh is a dedicated infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service communication. It offloads networking concerns from application code to a proxy layer.

The Sidecar Pattern deploys a proxy (typically Envoy) alongside each service instance. This sidecar handles:

  • Traffic Management: Load balancing, circuit breaking, retries, timeouts
  • Security: mTLS encryption between services, certificate rotation
  • Observability: Distributed tracing, metrics collection, access logging
  • Resilience: Automatic retries, fault injection, health-based routing

Popular meshes: Istio (most feature-rich), Linkerd (lightweight, Kubernetes-native), Consul Connect (HashiCorp), Kuma (CNCF).

Benefits: Developers don't need to implement retry logic, circuit breakers, or distributed tracing in their application code. Operations teams configure these centrally.

Trade-offs: Increased resource usage (each sidecar uses ~50MB RAM), operational complexity, debugging challenges (traffic flows through multiple proxies).
Service Mesh & Sidecar.code:
# Istio VirtualService: Traffic splitting
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  hosts:
    - order-service
  http:
    - match:
        - headers:
            x-canary:
              exact: "true"
      route:
        - destination:
            host: order-service
            subset: v2
          weight: 100
    - route:
        - destination:
            host: order-service
            subset: v1
          weight: 90
        - destination:
            host: order-service
            subset: v2
          weight: 10
---
# DestinationRule: Circuit breaking
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  host: order-service
  trafficPolicy:
    connectionPool:
      tcp:
        maxConnections: 100
      http:
        http1MaxPendingRequests: 10
        maxRequestsPerConnection: 10
    loadBalancer:
      simple: ROUND_ROBIN
    outlierDetection:
      consecutive5xxErrors: 5
      interval: 30s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s
      maxEjectionPercent: 50

Event-Driven Architecture.exp:
Event-Driven Architecture (EDA) is an architectural pattern where services communicate through asynchronous events. When something happens (an 'event'), the service publishes it to an event broker. Other services that care about that event consume it and react accordingly.

Core Concepts:

  • Event: A significant change in state (OrderCreated, PaymentReceived, ShipmentDelivered)
  • Producer: The service that publishes the event
  • Consumer: The service that subscribes to and processes the event
  • Event Broker: The middleware that routes events (Kafka, RabbitMQ, AWS EventBridge, NATS)
  • Topic/Channel: The named destination where events of a type are published

Benefits: Loose coupling (services don't know about each other), scalability (consumers can be added independently), resilience (producers don't wait for consumers), audit trail (events stored in order).

Challenges: Eventual consistency, debugging across services, schema evolution, duplicate events (at-least-once delivery), and maintaining event ordering.

The Outbox Pattern ensures reliable event publishing by writing events to a database table in the same transaction as the business operation, then a separate process publishes those events to the broker.

Saga Pattern.exp:
The Saga Pattern manages distributed transactions across microservices. Instead of a single ACID transaction (impossible across services), a saga is a sequence of local transactions where each step publishes an event that triggers the next step.

If a step fails, the saga runs compensating transactions to undo previous steps. This provides eventual consistency without distributed locks.

Two implementations:

  • Choreography: Each service publishes events that trigger the next service. Decentralized, simple for few services, but hard to track overall flow.
  • Orchestration: A central orchestrator (using Step Functions, Temporal, or a custom coordinator) tells each service what to do. More control, but introduces a single point of coordination.

Example saga: Order Processing

  1. Order Service: Create order (PENDING status)
  2. Payment Service: Reserve payment
  3. Inventory Service: Reserve items
  4. Shipping Service: Schedule shipment
  5. Order Service: Mark order as CONFIRMED

If payment fails, compensate with: release inventory, cancel order.

The SAGA pattern is essential for maintaining data consistency in microservices without distributed transactions (XA, 2PC).

CQRS Pattern.exp:
CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) separates read operations (Queries) from write operations (Commands). Instead of a single model for both reads and writes, CQRS uses separate models optimized for each purpose.

Benefits:

  • Read and write workloads can be scaled independently (many read replicas, few write primaries)
  • Read models can be denormalized for fast queries (no JOINs needed)
  • Write models focus on business rules and validation
  • Different data stores can be used (PostgreSQL for writes, Elasticsearch for reads)
  • Commands can be queued for async processing

When to use: Complex domains with different read/write patterns, systems where reads vastly outnumber writes, applications needing multiple read representations of the same data.

When not to use: Simple CRUD applications (CQRS adds complexity), domains where read and write models are already similar.

CQRS is often combined with Event Sourcing — the write model stores events, and the read model is derived by replaying events.

SQL vs NoSQL.exp:
Choosing between SQL and NoSQL databases is a fundamental system design decision:

SQL (Relational) Databases: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle

  • Strengths: ACID transactions, complex queries (JOINs), schema enforcement, strong consistency, maturity
  • Best for: Financial systems, e-commerce, any app requiring complex relationships and strong consistency
  • Schema: Fixed schema, migrations needed for changes

NoSQL Databases: MongoDB, DynamoDB, Cassandra, Redis, Couchbase

  • Types: Document (MongoDB), Key-Value (Redis), Wide-Column (Cassandra), Graph (Neo4j)
  • Strengths: Flexible schemas, horizontal scaling, high write throughput, specialized data models
  • Best for: Real-time apps, IoT, content management, catalogs, session stores
  • Trade-offs: Weaker consistency guarantees, limited query capabilities

Polyglot Persistence — using multiple database types within the same system, each for its strengths — is a common pattern in modern architectures. For example: PostgreSQL for orders (ACID), Redis for caching/sessions, MongoDB for product catalog (flexible schema), Elasticsearch for search.

Database Sharding.exp:
Sharding (horizontal partitioning) distributes data across multiple database instances. Each shard holds a subset of the data, and together they form the complete dataset.

Sharding Strategies:

  • Hash-Based: Shard = hash(shard_key) % N. Even distribution, but resharding is expensive (move data when N changes). Consistent hashing minimizes data movement during resharding.
  • Range-Based: Shard A = users 1-10000, Shard B = users 10001-20000. Good for range queries, but can cause hotspots if data isn't evenly distributed.
  • Directory-Based: A lookup table maps each key to its shard. Flexible but adds a lookup step.
  • Geographic: Data sharded by region (US, EU, APAC). Improves latency for regional users but complicates global queries.

Challenges:

  • Cross-shard queries: JOINs and transactions across shards are expensive or impossible
  • Resharding: Adding/removing shards requires data migration
  • Skew: Uneven data distribution can overload some shards
  • Secondary indexes: Indexes only exist within a shard

When to shard: Data size exceeds a single server's capacity (> 1TB), write throughput exceeds single node capacity, need geographic distribution. Start with replication/read replicas before sharding — sharding should be a last resort.

Database Replication.exp:
Database replication copies data from one database to another to improve availability, read performance, and disaster recovery.

Types:

  • Leader-Follower (Primary-Replica): One primary handles writes, replicas handle reads. Asynchronous replication (fast, eventual consistency) or synchronous (slower, strong consistency).
  • Leader-Leader (Multi-Primary): Multiple nodes accept writes. Complex conflict resolution is needed. Used in multi-region deployments.
  • Read Replicas: Elastically scale read capacity. Common pattern: one primary, many replicas for read-heavy workloads.

Replication Lag is the delay between a write on the primary and its appearance on a replica. This can cause issues where a user writes data, then reads from a replica that hasn't received the update yet (solved with read-your-writes consistency or always reading from primary for critical reads).

Best Practices:

  • Use read replicas for reporting, analytics, and dashboard queries
  • Route critical reads (after writes) to the primary
  • Monitor replication lag and set alerts
  • Use connection poolers (PgBouncer, ProxySQL) for efficient connection management

Connection Pooling.exp:
Connection pooling maintains a cache of database connections that can be reused across requests. Creating a new database connection for every request is expensive (TCP handshake, SSL negotiation, authentication).

Key parameters:

  • max (pool size): Maximum connections in the pool. Set based on: max_connections of DB, number of app instances, expected concurrent requests. Formula: (max_connections * 0.8) / app_instances.
  • min/idle: Minimum idle connections to maintain for quick responses
  • idleTimeoutMillis: Time before closing idle connections
  • connectionTimeoutMillis: Max wait time for a connection from the pool

When queries are too slow, check:

  1. Are we waiting for a connection from the pool? (pool exhaustion)
  2. Is the DB max_connections limit reached?
  3. Are there long-running queries blocking other queries?

Connection poolers like PgBouncer (PostgreSQL) and ProxySQL (MySQL) sit between the application and database, providing multiplexing and connection pooling at the network level — essential for serverless environments where many ephemeral connections are created.

Event Sourcing.exp:
Event Sourcing stores the state of an application as a sequence of events, rather than just the current state. Instead of updating a record (e.g., 'UPDATE balance SET amount = 100'), you append an event ('AccountCredited { amount: 100, timestamp: ... }'). The current state is derived by replaying all events.

Benefits:

  • Complete Audit Trail: Every state change is recorded forever. You can see exactly what happened and when.
  • Time Travel: You can reconstruct the state at any point in time by replaying events up to that point.
  • Temporal Queries: Answer questions like 'what was the state on this date?'
  • Event-Driven Integration: Events can be published to other services naturally

Challenges:

  • Event Store Size: Events accumulate forever — need efficient storage and snapshotting
  • Schema Evolution: Events are immutable — new code must handle old event formats
  • Complexity: Building and maintaining projections is more complex than CRUD
  • Eventually Consistent Queries: Read models lag behind writes (eventual consistency)

Snapshots store the current state at intervals to avoid replaying all events from the beginning.

Multi-Level Caching.exp:
Caching is a multi-layer strategy. Each layer has different characteristics — closer to the user (faster, smaller capacity) vs closer to the database (slower, larger capacity).

The Multi-Level Cache:

  1. Browser Cache: Private cache on the user's device. Cache-Control headers control what's cached and for how long. Extremely fast (local) but limited to that user.
  2. CDN Cache: Edge servers distributed globally. Cache static assets (images, JS, CSS) and sometimes dynamic content. Reduces latency and origin server load.
  3. Reverse Proxy Cache: Nginx, Varnish, or similar in front of application servers. Can cache full HTTP responses (microcaching for dynamic content).
  4. Application Cache: In-memory caches like Redis or Memcached. Stores serialized objects, query results, session data. Sub-millisecond access.
  5. Database Cache: Built-in buffer pools (InnoDB buffer pool, PostgreSQL shared buffers). Reduce disk I/O by keeping frequently accessed data in memory.

Cache hit ratio = cache hits / (cache hits + cache misses). Aim for >90% for well-optimized caches.

Caching Strategies.exp:
Choosing the right caching strategy depends on data characteristics and access patterns:

Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading):

  • Application checks cache first
  • Cache miss → load from database → store in cache → return
  • Writes: invalidate cache (delete), then update database
  • Pros: Only caches what's requested, resilient to cache failure
  • Cons: Cache miss penalty (3 round trips), stale data until first request after invalidation

Read-Through:

  • Cache layer sits between app and database
  • Cache miss → cache loads from database transparently
  • Simplifies application code

Write-Through:

  • Write to cache and database simultaneously
  • No stale data (cache always fresh)
  • Higher write latency (must write to both)

Write-Behind (Write-Back):

  • Write to cache immediately, async write to database
  • Very fast writes, but risk of data loss if cache fails before DB write
  • Good for high-write workloads

Cache Invalidation is the hardest problem in caching. Common approaches:

  • TTL (Time To Live): Data expires and is refreshed automatically
  • Write-Through: Update cache on writes (always fresh)
  • Event-Driven Invalidation: Publish invalidation events when data changes

Redis Caching Patterns.exp:
Redis is the most popular caching solution due to its in-memory speed and versatile data structures.

Common Redis Patterns:

1. Session Store:
Store user sessions with TTL. Fast reads/writes, automatic expiration, no need to involve the database for session operations.

2. Rate Limiting:
Use INCR + EXPIRE to count requests per time window. Multiple algorithms: Token Bucket, Sliding Window, Fixed Window.

3. Distributed Locking:
Use SET NX EX to acquire a lock. Critical for coordinating access to shared resources across multiple instances.

4. Leaderboard/Sorted Sets:
ZADD to add scores, ZREVRANGE for top N, ZINCRBY to update scores. Used for gaming leaderboards, trending topics, or time-series data.

5. Pub/Sub:
Lightweight message broadcasting. Use for real-time notifications, but Redis Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget — no message persistence.

6. Rate Limiter (Sliding Window):
Use sorted sets with timestamps as scores to count requests in a rolling window. More accurate than fixed window counters.

Memory Management: Redis has configurable eviction policies when memory is full: noeviction, allkeys-lru (most common), allkeys-lfu, volatile-ttl, volatile-lru.

Content Delivery Networks.exp:
A CDN (Content Delivery Network) is a geographically distributed network of proxy servers that cache content closer to users. This improves load times, reduces bandwidth costs, and increases content availability.

How CDNs work:

  1. User requests a resource (e.g., example.com/logo.png)
  2. DNS resolves to the nearest CDN edge server (PoP — Point of Presence)
  3. Edge server checks its cache: Cache HIT → serve immediately; Cache MISS → fetch from origin, cache, then serve
  4. Subsequent requests for the same resource are served from edge cache (fast)

What to cache on CDN:

  • Static assets: Images, CSS, JavaScript, fonts, videos (long TTL)
  • API responses: Public API data with Cache-Control headers
  • HTML pages: Either static HTML or dynamic pages with short TTL
  • Streaming content: Video on demand, live streams

Cache invalidation on CDN: Most CDNs support purging cached content by URL pattern, tags, or full invalidation. Purging is typically charged per request.

Leading CDN providers: Cloudflare, AWS CloudFront, Fastly, Akamai, Azure CDN, Google Cloud CDN. Edge computing platforms (Cloudflare Workers, Lambda@Edge) extend CDNs with serverless compute at the edge.

Message Queue Fundamentals.exp:
Message queues enable asynchronous communication between services. Producers send messages to a queue, and consumers process them. This decouples services and provides buffering during traffic spikes.

Key Concepts:

  • Producer: Application that sends messages
  • Consumer: Application that receives and processes messages
  • Queue: Buffer that stores messages until consumed
  • Exchange/Router: Routes messages to queues (in AMQP systems)
  • Binding: Links an exchange to a queue with a routing pattern

Delivery Guarantees:

  • At-Most-Once: Message may be lost but never redelivered (fast, lossy)
  • At-Least-Once: Message is guaranteed delivered, may be duplicated (needs idempotent consumers)
  • Exactly-Once: Message delivered exactly once (highest overhead, often approximated with deduplication)

Message Acknowledgment: Consumers explicitly acknowledge (ACK) successful processing. If a consumer fails without ACKing, the message is redelivered to another consumer. Dead Letter Queues (DLQ) capture messages that repeatedly fail processing.

Popular message brokers: RabbitMQ (AMQP), Apache Kafka (distributed streaming), AWS SQS/SNS, Google Pub/Sub, NATS, Redis Streams.

Apache Kafka.exp:
Apache Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform designed for high-throughput, fault-tolerant data pipelines. Unlike traditional message queues, Kafka persists all messages for a configurable retention period, enabling replay and multiple consumers.

Core Concepts:

  • Topic: A named stream of records (like a category/feed name)
  • Partition: A topic is split into partitions for parallelism. Each partition is an ordered, immutable sequence of records.
  • Offset: A unique ID of a record within a partition — consumers track their position
  • Broker: A Kafka server in the cluster
  • Consumer Group: A group of consumers that share the work of reading a topic. Each partition is consumed by exactly one consumer in the group.
  • Replication Factor: Number of copies of each partition across brokers (fault tolerance)

Key Differences from RabbitMQ:

  • Kafka persists messages (configurable retention: hours to forever); RabbitMQ deletes after consumption
  • Kafka is optimized for high throughput (millions of messages/sec); RabbitMQ has richer routing
  • Kafka's consumer groups enable multiple independent consumer applications; RabbitMQ queues are consumed
  • Kafka's log structure is ideal for event sourcing and stream processing

Use cases: Log aggregation, metrics collection, event sourcing, stream processing, change data capture (CDC), and data integration pipelines.

Event Sourcing with Kafka.exp:
Kafka's immutable log is a natural fit for Event Sourcing. Instead of storing current state in a database and publishing events separately, you store events directly in Kafka topics.

Change Data Capture (CDC) with tools like Debezium captures database changes as events and publishes them to Kafka. This enables event-driven integration without modifying existing applications — every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE in your database becomes an event.

Kafka Streams / ksqlDB enable real-time stream processing: transform, aggregate, join, and filter streams of events. For example, compute real-time sales totals, detect fraud patterns, or build materialized views.

Schema Registry manages Avro/Protobuf/JSON schemas for Kafka topics, ensuring producers and consumers use compatible formats. Schema evolution rules (forward/backward compatibility) prevent breaking changes.

Kafka's compaction feature (log compaction) keeps the latest value for each key while removing older duplicates — useful for 'table' semantics (e.g., the latest state of a user profile).

SQS & SNS (AWS).exp:
AWS provides two core messaging services:

SQS (Simple Queue Service) — Fully managed message queues:

  • Standard: Unlimited throughput, at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering
  • FIFO: Exactly-once processing, first-in-first-out delivery, up to 3000 msg/s (with batching)
  • Visibility timeout: Message becomes invisible while being processed. If not deleted within timeout, it reappears (redelivery).
  • Dead-Letter Queue: Configure maxReceiveCount — messages exceeding it go to DLQ
  • Long polling (ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds): Reduces empty responses

SNS (Simple Notification Service) — Pub/sub messaging:

  • Topics fan out messages to multiple subscribers (SQS, Lambda, HTTP, email, SMS)
  • Fan-out pattern: SNS → multiple SQS queues for parallel processing
  • Message filtering: Filter policies route only relevant messages to subscribers
  • FIFO topics: Strict ordering, exactly-once delivery to FIFO queues

Best Practice: Set appropriate visibility timeouts (longer than expected processing time). Always delete messages after processing (they reappear if not deleted!). Use DLQs with alarms for monitoring failed messages.

Consensus Algorithms.exp:
Consensus algorithms allow a group of nodes to agree on a value or state despite failures. They are fundamental to distributed systems — used in leader election, state machine replication, and distributed coordination.

Paxos (Leslie Lamport, 1989): The foundational consensus algorithm. Uses phases of prepare/promise (find a value) and accept/accepted (commit the value). Known for being notoriously difficult to understand and implement correctly.

Raft (Diego Ongaro, 2013): Designed for understandability. Key concepts:

  • Leader Election: Servers are in one of three states: Leader, Follower, or Candidate. Leaders send heartbeats; if followers don't hear from the leader, they start an election.
  • Log Replication: The leader accepts client requests, appends them to its log, and replicates them to followers. A log entry is committed once a majority of followers have acknowledged it.
  • Safety: At most one leader per term. A leader never overwrites its own log entries.

Real-world implementations: etcd (Raft, used by Kubernetes), Consul (Raft), ZooKeeper (Zab, similar to Paxos).

Distributed Transactions.exp:
In a monolithic application, a transaction can span multiple tables using ACID guarantees. In microservices, data is split across databases, making distributed transactions much harder.

Two-Phase Commit (2PC):

  1. Prepare Phase: Coordinator asks all participants to prepare (vote). Each participant writes the transaction to a write-ahead log but doesn't commit.
  2. Commit Phase: If all vote YES, coordinator broadcasts COMMIT. If any votes NO, broadcasts ABORT.

2PC provides strong consistency but has problems: blocking (participants hold locks while waiting for coordinator), and coordinator failure (participants are stuck in prepared state).

The Saga Pattern (described earlier) is the preferred alternative for microservices. It sacrifices immediate consistency for eventual consistency:

  • Each service performs its own local transaction
  • On success, it publishes an event triggering the next step
  • On failure, compensating transactions undo previous steps

When to use each:

  • 2PC: When strong consistency is absolutely required (financial systems, inventory allocation). Use sparingly — most modern systems avoid 2PC.
  • Saga: Most microservices scenarios. Provides good enough consistency with much better availability and performance.
  • Outbox Pattern: Ensures database operations and event publishing are atomic — essential for reliable event-driven architectures.

Distributed Tracing.exp:
Distributed tracing follows a request as it travels through multiple services in a microservices architecture. It's essential for debugging performance issues and errors in distributed systems.

Key Concepts:

  • Trace: Represents the entire journey of a request across all services
  • Span: A single unit of work within a trace (one API call, one DB query, one queue operation)
  • Trace ID: Propagated across service boundaries via HTTP headers (traceparent, baggage)
  • Span Context: Parent-child relationships between spans
  • Sampling: Not all requests are traced (head-based: sample at entry; tail-based: sample based on criteria like errors)

OpenTelemetry is the industry standard for instrumentation. It provides SDKs for all major languages and supports exporting traces to multiple backends (Jaeger, Zipkin, Grafana Tempo, Datadog, Honeycomb).

Common issues revealed by distributed tracing:

  • Unexpected service dependencies
  • High latency in specific service calls
  • Database query bottlenecks
  • Error propagation patterns
  • Hotspots under load

Distributed Locking.exp:
Distributed locks coordinate access to shared resources across multiple application instances. Without them, concurrent requests can cause race conditions, data corruption, or duplicate operations.

When you need distributed locks:

  • Scheduled tasks that should run on only one instance (cron jobs)
  • Graceful shutdown/restart coordination
  • Rate limiting across instances
  • Accessing shared resources (writing to the same file, consuming from a queue)
  • Idempotency checks (process a payment only once)

Redis-based locks (SET NX): Simple, fast, but not perfectly safe (lock can expire while process is still running — use Redlock algorithm for stricter safety).

etcd/ZooKeeper-based locks: Stronger guarantees via consensus protocols. Use for critical coordination where safety matters more than speed.

Database-based locks: Use SELECT FOR UPDATE or advisory locks. Simple but slower and more database load.

Important: Always set a TTL (lease time) on locks so they auto-release if the holder crashes. Use a unique lock ID (UUID) so only the lock owner can release it. Implement retry with backoff for lock acquisition.

Load Balancing Algorithms.exp:
Load balancers distribute incoming requests across multiple backend servers to maximize throughput, minimize response time, and avoid overloading any single server.

Algorithms:

  • Round Robin: Requests distributed sequentially. Simple but doesn't account for server load or capacity differences.
  • Least Connections: Sends to server with fewest active connections. Better for requests with varying processing times.
  • Least Response Time: Sends to server with fastest response time + fewest connections (combined metric).
  • IP Hash: Consistent routing based on client IP (or a portion of it). Useful for session persistence (sticky sessions).
  • Weighted: Each server gets a weight (e.g., server A: weight 3, server B: weight 1) — higher weight receives more traffic. Useful when servers have different capacities.
  • Random: Picks a random server with optional weights. Good for large, homogeneous pools.

Health Checks: Load balancers periodically check server health (HTTP, TCP, or custom). Unhealthy servers are removed from the pool. Common checks: /health endpoint, TCP port check, or custom script.

Session Persistence (Sticky Sessions): Ensures a user's requests go to the same server. Implemented via cookies, IP hash, or session affinity. However, sticky sessions make horizontal scaling harder — prefer stateless applications that externalize session data to Redis.

Circuit Breaker Pattern.exp:
The Circuit Breaker pattern prevents cascading failures in distributed systems. When a service call fails repeatedly, the circuit breaker 'opens' and subsequent calls fail immediately (without attempting the call), allowing the downstream service time to recover.

Three States:

  • CLOSED: Normal operation. Requests pass through. If failures exceed threshold, move to OPEN.
  • OPEN: Requests fail immediately. After a timeout, move to HALF-OPEN to test if service has recovered.
  • HALF-OPEN: A limited number of requests are allowed through. If they succeed, move to CLOSED. If they fail, back to OPEN.

When to use: When calling external APIs, third-party services, databases, or any service that might become slow or unavailable. Especially important when the failing service could cascade (e.g., a slow database causing API servers to exhaust their connection pools).

Best practices:

  • Set appropriate thresholds and timeouts based on your SLAs
  • Log all circuit state changes for debugging
  • Consider partial degradation: when circuit is open, return cached or default data
  • Monitor circuit state in dashboards
  • Combine with retries and timeouts for complete resilience

Popular implementations: Resilience4j (Java), Polly (.NET), and custom implementations for Node.js/Python.

Bulkhead Pattern.exp:
The Bulkhead Pattern isolates components of a system so that failure in one component doesn't cascade to others. It's named after the bulkhead compartments on ships — if one compartment is breached, the others remain watertight.

Implementation approaches:

  • Thread Pool Isolation: Each service/client gets its own thread pool. If one pool is exhausted (blocked on slow external service), other pools remain unaffected.
  • Connection Pool Isolation: Separate connection pools for different services or database types. A spike in one area doesn't starve other areas.
  • Semaphore Isolation: Limit concurrent calls to any one service using semaphores (lighter than thread pools).

Example: Your application calls the Payment service, Inventory service, and Email service. Without bulkheads, if Payment becomes slow and exhausts the shared connection pool, ALL requests fail (including those that don't need Payment). With bulkheads, only Payment-related operations are affected.

Bulkhead sizes should be tuned based on expected concurrency for each component. Setting them too small causes artificial blocking; too large defeats the purpose.

Bulkheads are often combined with Circuit Breakers for complete resilience: the bulkhead limits concurrent calls, and the circuit breaker cuts off calls entirely when failure rates are high.

Retry & Backoff.exp:
Transient failures (network timeouts, service temporarily unavailable, database deadlocks) are common in distributed systems. The Retry pattern handles these by reattempting the failed operation.

Exponential Backoff: Instead of retrying immediately (which could overwhelm an already struggling service), increase the delay between retries exponentially: 100ms, 200ms, 400ms, 800ms, 1600ms...

Jitter: Add randomness to the delay to prevent the 'thundering herd' problem where all clients retry simultaneously. For example: delay = base * (2^attempt) + random(0, 100).

Retry Budget: Limit total retries within a time window. If 10% of requests result in retries, stop retrying and fail fast — the system is likely overloaded.

When NOT to retry:

  • 4xx errors (client's fault — won't succeed on retry)
  • Requests that modify state without idempotency guarantees
  • When the total request time would exceed your SLA

Idempotency: Ensure retried requests have the same effect as a single request. Use idempotency keys (idempotency-key header) that the server deduplicates.

Combine retries with circuit breakers: retry a few times, then open the circuit to give the service breathing room.

RESTful API Design.exp:
REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for designing networked applications. Key principles:

Resource Naming:

  • Use nouns, not verbs: /users (not /getUsers)
  • Plural for collections: /users, /orders
  • Hierarchical: /users/:id/orders/:orderId
  • Query parameters for filtering: /orders?status=pending&page=1

HTTP Methods:

  • GET — Retrieve resources (idempotent, safe)
  • POST — Create resources (non-idempotent)
  • PUT — Full replacement (idempotent)
  • PATCH — Partial update
  • DELETE — Remove resource (idempotent)

HTTP Status Codes:

  • 200 OK — Successful GET, PUT, PATCH
  • 201 Created — Successful POST
  • 204 No Content — Successful DELETE
  • 400 Bad Request — Invalid input
  • 401 Unauthorized — Missing/invalid auth
  • 403 Forbidden — Insufficient permissions
  • 404 Not Found — Resource doesn't exist
  • 409 Conflict — Version conflict, duplicate
  • 429 Too Many Requests — Rate limited
  • 500 Internal Server Error — Unexpected failure

Best Practices: Version your API (/api/v1/users), use pagination (cursor or offset-based), include error details in response body, use consistent naming conventions (snake_case or camelCase), and document with OpenAPI.

API Rate Limiting.exp:
Rate limiting controls how often clients can call your API to prevent abuse, ensure fair usage, and protect backend resources.

Algorithms:

  • Token Bucket: Tokens added at a fixed rate. Each request consumes a token. If no tokens available, request is rejected. Supports bursts (up to bucket capacity).
  • Fixed Window: Count requests in fixed time windows (e.g., 100 requests per hour). Simple but allows bursts at window boundaries (100 requests at 11:59 + 100 at 12:00 = 200 in 1 minute).
  • Sliding Window Log: Track timestamps of each request. Count requests in the last N seconds. Accurate but memory-intensive.
  • Sliding Window Counter: A hybrid: count requests in the current window + approximate from the previous window. Most common in production (used by Kong, Stripe, GitHub).

Response headers (standard with rate limiting):

  • X-RateLimit-Limit — Max requests allowed in the window
  • X-RateLimit-Remaining — Requests remaining in the current window
  • X-RateLimit-Reset — Time (Unix timestamp) when the window resets
  • Retry-After — Seconds to wait before retrying (on 429 response)

Rate limiting tiers: Apply different limits based on plan (free: 100/hr, pro: 1000/hr), endpoint sensitivity (auth endpoints: stricter), and API key type.

API Versioning.exp:
API versioning allows you to evolve your API without breaking existing clients. When you need to change an API contract (add required fields, change response format, remove endpoints), a new version lets old clients continue working.

Approaches:

  • URL Versioning (/api/v1/users): Most common. Explicit, easy to route. Can clutter URLs and lead to code duplication.
  • Header Versioning (Accept: application/vnd.myapp.v1+json): Clean URLs, but harder to test and debug (version is 'hidden').
  • Query Parameter Versioning (/api/users?version=1): Simple but can be accidentally omitted.
  • Content Negotiation: Version based on Accept header media type.

Best Practices:

  • Version from day one, even if you don't expect breaking changes
  • Support each version for a reasonable period (6-12 months)
  • Provide clear deprecation notices in response headers (Sunset, Deprecation)
  • Maintain old versions as thin translation layers (adapter pattern)
  • Communicate breaking changes well in advance
  • Use semantic versioning for your API (major = breaking change)

When NOT to version: Adding optional fields, changing internal implementation, or fixing bugs that don't change the contract. These are backward-compatible changes.

GraphQL Fundamentals.exp:
GraphQL is a query language for APIs developed by Meta. Clients request exactly the data they need, eliminating over-fetching and under-fetching problems common with REST.

Core Concepts:

  • Schema: Defines types, queries, mutations, and subscriptions using SDL (Schema Definition Language)
  • Query: Fetch data (equivalent to GET)
  • Mutation: Modify data (equivalent to POST/PUT/DELETE)
  • Subscription: Real-time data via WebSockets
  • Resolver: Function that fetches data for a field
  • N+1 Problem: GraphQL can trigger many database queries for nested fields. Solved with DataLoader (batching + caching).

Benefits over REST:

  • Clients control exactly what data they receive
  • Single endpoint (/graphql) replaces many REST endpoints
  • Strongly typed: self-documenting schema
  • Introspection: tools like GraphiQL auto-generate documentation

When to use GraphQL: Complex frontends with varying data needs, multiple client types (web, mobile), rapid iteration with changing requirements.

When REST is better: Simple CRUD APIs, caching at HTTP level (GraphQL uses a single POST endpoint, making CDN caching harder), file uploads.

Many systems use both: GraphQL for frontend queries, REST/gRPC for backend service-to-service communication.

URL Shortener.exp:
Problem: Design a URL shortening service like bit.ly or TinyURL. Users enter a long URL and get a short, unique alias. Visiting the short URL redirects to the original long URL.

Requirements:

  • Generate a unique, short alias (6-7 characters) for each URL
  • Redirect users when they visit a short URL (301 redirect)
  • Handle millions of URLs and billions of redirects
  • Optional: expiration, analytics (click count, referrer), custom aliases

Key Design Decisions:

  • Encoding: Base62 (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) = 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion unique combinations
  • ID Generation: Use a distributed ID generator (Snowflake, Redis INCR) or hash + collision resolution
  • Storage: Store mapping in a fast key-value store (Redis) with database persistence
  • Redirection: 301 redirects are cached by browsers; store in CDN for popular URLs
  • Caching: LRU cache for frequently accessed URLs (reduce DB load)

Scale considerations: Write-heavy (URL creation), but astronomically read-heavy (redirects). Cache aggressively. Use CDN for popular short URLs. Consider async analytics (publish click events to Kafka, batch-process for stats).

Chat System.exp:
Problem: Design a real-time chat system like WhatsApp, Slack, or Discord. Users can send messages to individuals or groups, see online status, and receive push notifications.

Architecture:

  • WebSocket Connections: Persistent, bidirectional connections for real-time messaging. Use a WebSocket server that handles millions of concurrent connections.
  • Message Flow: Sender → WebSocket → Message Service → Store in DB → Publish to Queue → Fan out to recipients' connections
  • Horizontal Scaling: Use Redis Pub/Sub to broadcast messages across WebSocket server instances. When a user sends a message, the receiving server publishes it to Redis, and all servers receive the notification for any connected recipients.
  • Message Storage: Time-series database (Cassandra, ScyllaDB) for messages. Partition by conversation_id, ordered by timestamp. Messages are immutable.
  • Last Seen / Presence: Timestamps stored in Redis with heartbeat mechanism. Show 'online', 'recently', or exact timestamp.

Key challenges:

  • Exactly-once delivery: Use message IDs for deduplication
  • Offline messages: Store in queue; deliver when user comes online
  • Typing indicators: Send ephemeral events via WebSocket (not stored)
  • File sharing: Upload to S3/CDN, share URL in message
  • Push notifications: When user is offline, send push via FCM/APNs

Distributed File Storage.exp:
Problem: Design a distributed file storage system like Google Drive, Dropbox, or S3. Users upload, download, and share files with high durability and availability.

Key Requirements:

  • Store large files (up to 5TB) with high durability (99.999999999%)
  • Handle millions of concurrent uploads/downloads
  • Global availability with low latency
  • Versioning and conflict resolution
  • Access control (sharing permissions)

Architecture:

  • Upload Flow: Client → Load Balancer → Upload Service → Chunk the file → Store chunks across storage nodes → Update metadata DB + chunk index
  • Download Flow: Client → CDN (for popular files) or Download Service → Read chunk metadata → Fetch chunks → Reassemble → Stream to client
  • Storage Nodes: Commodity servers with large HDDs. Files are split into fixed-size chunks (e.g., 64MB) with erasure coding for redundancy (12+4 scheme: 12 data chunks + 4 parity chunks, tolerating 4 simultaneous failures).
  • Metadata Service: Stores file metadata (name, size, owner, permissions, creation date, chunk locations). Needs strong consistency (use a relational DB or a strongly consistent NoSQL store).
  • Chunk Store: Key-value store mapping chunk_id → binary blob. Use consistent hashing to distribute chunks across storage nodes.

Design patterns used: Erasure coding (better space efficiency than replication), consistent hashing (for chunk placement), eventual consistency for metadata, CDN caching for popular files, async indexing for search.

Payment System.exp:
Problem: Design a payment processing system like Stripe or PayPal that handles millions of transactions securely and reliably.

Critical Requirements:

  • Exactly-Once Processing: Never charge a customer twice. Use idempotency keys.
  • Atomicity: Money is either debited from sender AND credited to receiver, or neither happens.
  • Durability: Never lose a transaction record.
  • Auditability: Every transaction has a complete, immutable trail.
  • Security: PCI-DSS compliance, encrypted data, tokenization (never handle raw card numbers).

Architecture:

  • Payment Service: Orchestrates the payment flow. Validates input, calls PSPs (Payment Service Providers), updates transaction status.
  • Transaction Database: Each transaction has states: INITIATED → PROCESSING → SUCCEEDED / FAILED. Immutable event log.
  • Idempotency Store: Deduplicates requests using idempotency-key. If same key received, return cached result.
  • PSP Adapters: Abstraction layer for different payment providers (Stripe, PayPal, Adyen).

Payment Flow:

  1. Client sends payment request with idempotency key
  2. Payment Service validates (amount, currency, fraud check)
  3. Creates transaction record (INITIATED)
  4. Calls PSP with tokenized payment details
  5. PSP returns success/failure
  6. Update transaction status
  7. Publish PaymentCompleted/PaymentFailed event
  8. Other services react (update order status, send email)

Saga for multi-step: A payment might involve: reserve funds (auth) → capture → settle → transfer to merchant. If any step fails, run compensations (reverse the auth/capture).

Infrastructure as Code.exp:
Infrastructure as Code (IaC) manages cloud resources through machine-readable definition files instead of manual configuration. This enables version control, reproducibility, automation, and self-documenting infrastructure.

Key Benefits:

  • Reproducibility: Spin up identical environments (dev, staging, production) from the same code
  • Version Control: Infrastructure changes go through code review, just like application code
  • Auditability: Complete history of who changed what and when
  • Automation: CI/CD pipelines can create/destroy environments automatically
  • Self-Documentation: The code IS the documentation — always up to date

Popular IaC Tools:

  • Terraform (HashiCorp): Multi-cloud, declarative HCL language, state management
  • Pulumi: Use general-purpose languages (TS, Python, Go, C#) to define infrastructure
  • AWS CDK: Define AWS infrastructure using familiar programming languages
  • CloudFormation: AWS-native, YAML/JSON templates
  • Ansible: Configuration management (not just provisioning), agentless

Best Practices:

  • Store state files remotely (S3 + DynamoDB for Terraform)
  • Use modules to encapsulate reusable infrastructure patterns
  • Tag all resources for cost tracking and management
  • Use workspaces or directories for environment separation
  • Run plan/validate in CI as a mandatory step

Container Orchestration.exp:
Container orchestration automates the deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. Kubernetes (K8s) is the dominant platform.

Kubernetes Core Concepts:

  • Pod: The smallest deployable unit — one or more containers sharing network and storage
  • Deployment: Declarative management of Pods (rolling updates, scaling, self-healing)
  • Service: Stable network endpoint to access Pods (with load balancing)
  • ConfigMap/Secret: Configuration injected into Pods as environment variables or volumes
  • Ingress: External HTTP/S access with routing rules and TLS termination
  • Namespace: Virtual cluster for resource isolation

Deployment Strategies:

  • Rolling Update: Gradually replace old Pods with new ones (default)
  • Blue-Green: Two identical environments; switch traffic overnight
  • Canary: Route small percentage of traffic to new version
  • A/B Testing: Route specific users based on headers/cookies

Auto-scaling: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) scales based on CPU/memory or custom metrics. Cluster Autoscaler adds/removes nodes.

Alternatives: Docker Swarm (simpler, less features), Nomad (HashiCorp, simpler than K8s), AWS ECS (managed, AWS-specific).
Container Orchestration.code:
# Kubernetes deployment manifests

# deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-server
  namespace: production
  labels:
    app: api-server
    tier: backend
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0  # Zero-downtime deployment
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api-server
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api-server
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: myregistry.azurecr.io/api-server:1.2.3
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
          env:
            - name: NODE_ENV
              value: "production"
            - name: DATABASE_URL
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: app-secrets
                  key: database-url
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
            limits:
              cpu: 500m
              memory: 512Mi
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 3000
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
            periodSeconds: 10
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 3000
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 5
---
# service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api-server
  namespace: production
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: api-server
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 3000
---
# hpa.yaml (auto-scaling)
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: api-server
  namespace: production
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: api-server
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: memory
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 80

CI/CD Pipeline Design.exp:
CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery) automates building, testing, and deploying your application.

Continuous Integration: Developers merge code changes frequently (multiple times daily) into a shared main branch. Each merge triggers automated builds and tests to catch integration issues early.

Continuous Delivery: Code changes are automatically built, tested, and prepared for release to production. Deployment to production may be manual (with a button push).

Continuous Deployment: Every change that passes all stages of the pipeline is automatically deployed to production — no human intervention.

Pipeline Stages:

  1. Source: Trigger on push/PR to main branch
  2. Build: Compile code, install dependencies, build artifacts/Docker image
  3. Test: Run unit tests, integration tests, linting, type checking, security scan
  4. Staging Deploy: Deploy to staging environment (identical to production)
  5. Smoke Tests: Quick tests to verify the deployment worked
  6. Approval Gate (optional): Manual approval before production
  7. Production Deploy: Deploy with rollout strategy (blue-green, canary, rolling)
  8. Post-Deploy: Run smoke tests, monitor metrics, rollback if needed

    9. Tools: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD, Jenkins, CircleCI, Buildkite, ArgoCD (GitOps for K8s).
CI/CD Pipeline Design.code:
# GitHub Actions complete CI/CD workflow
name: Deploy to Production

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

env:
  REGISTRY: ghcr.io
  IMAGE_NAME: ${{ github.repository }}
  NODE_VERSION: '20'

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16-alpine
        env:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: testpass
        options: >-
          --health-cmd pg_isready
          --health-interval 10s
      redis:
        image: redis:7-alpine
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "redis-cli ping"
          --health-interval 10s

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ env.NODE_VERSION }}
          cache: 'npm'

      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run typecheck
      - run: npm run test:unit
      - run: npm run test:integration
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:testpass@localhost:5432/test
          REDIS_URL: redis://localhost:6379
      - name: Security audit
        run: npm audit --audit-level=high

  build:
    needs: [test]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ${{ env.REGISTRY }}
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          push: true
          tags: |
            ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }}
            ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:latest
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

  deploy-staging:
    needs: [build]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: |
          kubectl set image deployment/api-server \
            app=${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }} \
            --namespace=staging
          kubectl rollout status deployment/api-server --namespace=staging

  deploy-production:
    needs: [deploy-staging]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: production
      url: https://app.example.com
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: |
          kubectl set image deployment/api-server \
            app=${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }} \
            --namespace=production
          kubectl rollout status deployment/api-server --namespace=production

      - name: Post-deploy smoke test
        run: |
          curl -f https://app.example.com/health
          curl -f https://app.example.com/api/v1/status

Monitoring & Observability Stack.exp:
Observability is the ability to understand a system's internal state from its external outputs (logs, metrics, traces). It's essential for operating distributed systems at scale.

The Three Pillars:

1. Logging: Discrete events with timestamps. Structured (JSON) logs enable searching and filtering. Centralized log aggregation (ELK, Loki, Datadog) correlates logs across services.

2. Metrics: Numerical measurements collected over time. Key metrics (RED method for services):

  • Rate: Requests per second
  • Errors: Failed requests / total requests
  • Duration: Latency distribution (p50, p95, p99)

Key metrics (USE method for resources):

  • Utilization: % time resource is busy (CPU, memory, disk I/O)
  • Saturation: Queue length or contention
  • Errors: Count of error events

3. Distributed Tracing: Follows a request through all services. Essential for debugging latency issues and understanding service dependencies.

Recommended Stack:

  • Prometheus — Metrics collection and alerting
  • Grafana — Dashboards and visualization
  • OpenTelemetry — Instrumentation (traces + metrics)
  • Loki / Elasticsearch — Log storage and query
  • Jaeger / Grafana Tempo — Distributed tracing backend
  • AlertManager — Alert routing and notification

version: '3.8'
services:
  # Metrics
  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus:v2.51.0
    volumes:
      - ./prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
      - prometheus_data:/prometheus
    ports:
      - '9090:9090'

  # Dashboards
  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana:10.2.3

      - ./grafana/datasources:/etc/grafana/provisioning/datasources
    ports:

    command: -config.file=/etc/tempo.yaml
    volumes:
      - ./tempo.yaml:/etc/tempo.yaml
      - tempo_data:/tmp/tempo

volumes:

# Application-level metrics
const prometheus = require('prom-client');

const httpRequestDuration = new prometheus.Histogram({
  name: 'http_request_duration_seconds',
  help: 'Duration of HTTP requests in seconds',
  labelNames: ['method', 'route', 'status'],
  buckets: [0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 5]
});

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  const end = httpRequestDuration.startTimer();
  res.on('finish', () => {
    end({ method: req.method, route: req.route?.path || 'unknown', status: res.statusCode });
  });
  next();
});

app.get('/metrics', async (req, res) => {
  res.set('Content-Type', prometheus.register.contentType);
  res.end(await prometheus.register.metrics());
});
